_comment: CloudWatch alarms for RITHM Phase 1. Applied by ops/scripts/put-alarms.sh, which
substitutes ${VAR} placeholders from the environment and calls put-metric-alarm once
per entry. put-metric-alarm is upsert-by-name, so re-running is a no-op.
Six alarms, not fifteen. Each one names a failure that is otherwise SILENT — the
system keeps answering 200s while users get nothing. Alarms for things you would
notice anyway are how people learn to ignore their inbox.
Shaped for the Day-5 always-on-GPU decision: rithm-worker-poc runs 24/7, so 'the GPU
has been running too long' (the parent plan's third alarm) is the steady state. What
matters instead is the box or the ACE-Step process dying.

alarms.AlarmDescription: A generation job failed 3 SQS receives and was dead-lettered. The user's track is gone and nothing else in the system says so. Runbook: ops/runbooks/dlq-drain.md

THE WORST SILENT FAILURE IN THE SYSTEM. The worker finished, the track is in S3, the GPU time is spent -- and the completion never reached the API, so the user watches a spinner forever. Runbook: ops/runbooks/dlq-drain.md

The oldest queued job has waited over 10 minutes. The single best 'generation is broken' signal: catches a dead worker, a dead ACE-Step server, and a wedged DB claim all at once. Real wall-clock is ~15s per job, so 600s means nothing is draining. Runbook: ops/runbooks/worker-stuck.md

The always-on GPU box failed an EC2 status check. Every generation fails while this is true. Carries an ec2:recover action so the common case (degraded underlying host) self-heals before a human reads the email.
The API returned more than 5 server errors in 5 minutes. It is the only path to every feature, so this is user-visible breakage regardless of which module threw.

Zero healthy API targets. desiredCount is pinned at 1 because SSE pub/sub is in-process, so one unhealthy host is a total outage -- not a degraded fleet. TreatMissingData is 'breaching': no data from a target group is itself the bad news.
